statement: Let $f\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be [continuous](c:continuous-function) and [integrable](c:integrable-function), and let its [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) $\hat f(\xi) = \int f(x)\, e^{-2\pi i x \cdot \xi}\, dx$ also be integrable. Then $f(x) = \int \hat f(\xi)\, e^{2\pi i x \cdot \xi}\, d\xi$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).
The function $f$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function) on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) $\hat f$ is integrable on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

conclusion: The inverse transform of $\hat f$ equals $f$ at every point: $f(x) = \int \hat f(\xi)\, e^{2\pi i x \cdot \xi}\, d\xi$.

formal.difference: The declaration works on any finite-dimensional real inner product space, with values in any complete complex normed space. It states the identity as an equality of functions, $\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\mathcal{F} f) = f$.

proofs.name: Gaussian regularization
proofs.slogan: Damp the inverse transform by a Gaussian factor, move the transform onto the damped exponential, and let the resulting narrow kernels concentrate at the point.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem at each point $x$; the proof uses continuity of $f$ only at $x$. On the [Schwartz space](c:schwartz-space) all hypotheses hold, so the transform is invertible there.

roles.why: Integrability of $\hat f$ gives the dominating function that removes the Gaussian factor in the limit.
Integrability of $f$ justifies the exchange of integrals and controls the far part of the kernel integral.
Continuity of $f$ at $x$ makes the kernel averages converge to $f(x)$.

steps.slogan: Insert the Gaussian factor $e^{-|\xi|^2/c}$ into the inverse transform integral.
steps.detail: Let $I_c(x) = \int \hat f(\xi)\, e^{-|\xi|^2/c}\, e^{2\pi i x \cdot \xi}\, d\xi$ for $c > 0$. The factor tends to $1$ as $c \to \infty$ and is bounded by $1$, and $\hat f$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function), so dominated convergence gives $I_c(x) \to \int \hat f(\xi)\, e^{2\pi i x \cdot \xi}\, d\xi$.

steps.slogan: Move the transform from $f$ to the damped exponential by Fubini's theorem.
steps.detail: For integrable $\varphi$ and $f$, both $\int \varphi \hat f$ and $\int \hat\varphi f$ equal the absolutely convergent double integral $\iint \varphi(\xi) f(y)\, e^{-2\pi i y \cdot \xi}\, dy\, d\xi$. With $\varphi(\xi) = e^{-|\xi|^2/c} e^{2\pi i x \cdot \xi}$ this gives $I_c(x) = \int \hat\varphi(y) f(y)\, dy$.

steps.slogan: Compute the transform of the damped exponential as a narrow Gaussian centered at $x$.
steps.detail: Completing the square and the [Gaussian integral](c:gaussian-integral) give $\hat\varphi(y) = K_c(x - y)$ with $K_c(z) = (\pi c)^{n/2} e^{-\pi^2 c |z|^2}$. Each $K_c$ is positive with total integral $1$, and its mass outside any ball around $0$ tends to $0$ as $c \to \infty$.

steps.slogan: Show that the kernel averages $\int K_c(x - y) f(y)\, dy$ tend to $f(x)$.
steps.detail: The difference is $\int K_c(x - y)(f(y) - f(x))\, dy$. On a small ball around $x$ the factor $|f(y) - f(x)|$ is small by [continuity](c:continuous-function) at $x$; outside it, $K_c$ is uniformly small against the integrable $f$ and has small mass against the constant $f(x)$.

steps.slogan: Equate the two limits of $I_c(x)$ to get the inversion formula.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 4 give two limits of the same quantity $I_c(x)$ as $c \to \infty$. Limits are unique, so $\int \hat f(\xi)\, e^{2\pi i x \cdot \xi}\, d\xi = f(x)$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity at $x$ lets the concentrating kernels recover the value $f(x)$.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability of $f$ and $\hat f$ justifies dominated convergence and Fubini.
concepts.c:fourier-transform: The proof inverts the transform by passing it from $f$ to a Gaussian.
concepts.c:schwartz-space: Schwartz functions satisfy every hypothesis, so inversion holds on that space.
concepts.c:gaussian-integral: The Gaussian integral normalizes the kernels to total mass one.

statement: Let $f\colon [a, b] \to E$ be [continuous](c:continuous-function), with values in a real [normed space](c:normed-space) $E$ and with right [derivative](c:derivative) $f'(x)$ at each $x \in [a, b)$. If $\|f(a)\| \le \delta$ and $\|f'(x)\| \le K\|f(x)\| + \varepsilon$ on $[a, b)$, then $\|f(x)\| \le \delta e^{K(x-a)} + \frac{\varepsilon}{K}(e^{K(x-a)} - 1)$ on $[a, b]$, read as $\delta + \varepsilon(x - a)$ when $K = 0$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f\colon [a, b] \to E$ into a real [normed space](c:normed-space) is [continuous](c:continuous-function).
At each $x \in [a, b)$, the map $f$ has the right [derivative](c:derivative) $f'(x)$.
The initial value satisfies $\|f(a)\| \le \delta$.
The [differential inequality](c:differential-inequality) $\|f'(x)\| \le K\|f(x)\| + \varepsilon$ holds for every $x \in [a, b)$.

conclusion: For every $x \in [a, b]$, $\|f(x)\|$ is at most the Grönwall bound $\delta e^{K(x-a)} + \frac{\varepsilon}{K}(e^{K(x-a)} - 1)$, or $\delta + \varepsilon(x - a)$ when $K = 0$.

proofs.name: Comparison with a barrier solution
proofs.slogan: Bound the right slopes of $\|f\|$, compare $\|f\|$ with the exact solution of $\varphi' = K\varphi + \varepsilon'$, and let $\varepsilon'$ decrease to $\varepsilon$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for all real $\delta$, $K$ and $\varepsilon$, including $K = 0$ and negative $K$. At $x = a$ the bound is $\delta$, which is the initial hypothesis.

roles.why: Continuity makes $u = \|f\|$ continuous, so the set where $u$ stays below the barrier is closed.
The right derivative controls the right difference quotients of $f$.
The initial bound puts the left end $a$ below the barrier.
The [differential inequality](c:differential-inequality) bounds the growth rate of $u$ by $Ku + \varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Bound the right slopes of the norm $u = \|f\|$ by $Ku + \varepsilon$.
steps.detail: The reverse triangle inequality gives $|u(z) - u(x)| \le \|f(z) - f(x)\|$. Hence the lower right slope of $u$ at $x \in [a, b)$ is at most $\|f'(x)\| \le K u(x) + \varepsilon$, and $u$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $[a, b]$.

steps.slogan: Solve the comparison equation $\varphi' = K\varphi + \varepsilon'$ with $\varphi(a) = \delta$ for each $\varepsilon' > \varepsilon$.
steps.detail: The function $\varphi(x) = \delta e^{K(x-a)} + \frac{\varepsilon'}{K}(e^{K(x-a)} - 1)$, or $\delta + \varepsilon'(x - a)$ if $K = 0$, is built from the [exponential function](c:exponential-function). Differentiation gives $\varphi(a) = \delta$ and $\varphi' = K\varphi + \varepsilon'$.

steps.slogan: Show that $u$ stays below the barrier $\varphi$ on all of $[a, b]$.
steps.detail: The set $S = \{x \in [a, b] : u(x) \le \varphi(x)\}$ is closed and contains $a$. At a point of $S$ with $u = \varphi$, the slopes of $u$ fall below $Ku + \varepsilon < \varphi'$ arbitrarily close on the right, and where $u < \varphi$ continuity keeps $u < \varphi$ nearby; so $S$ meets every interval to the right of its points, and $S = [a, b]$.

steps.slogan: Let $\varepsilon'$ decrease to $\varepsilon$ in the barrier bound.
steps.detail: For fixed $x$ the barrier value is continuous in $\varepsilon'$. The bounds $u(x) \le \varphi_{\varepsilon'}(x)$ for all $\varepsilon' > \varepsilon$ pass to the limit and give the Grönwall bound with $\varepsilon$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of $\|f\|$ makes the comparison set closed.
concepts.c:normed-space: The norm turns the vector-valued problem into a scalar inequality.
concepts.c:derivative: The right derivative bounds the right slopes of the norm.
concepts.c:differential-inequality: The differential inequality is the growth bound that the barrier dominates.
concepts.c:exponential-function: The barrier solution of the linear equation is exponential.

statement: If $R$ is a commutative [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring), then the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $R[x]$ is Noetherian. In particular, every [ideal](c:ideal) of $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ over a [field](c:field) $k$ is finitely generated.

hypotheses.text: The commutative ring $R$ is [Noetherian](c:noetherian-ring): every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated.

conclusion: Every [ideal](c:ideal) of $R[x]$, and of $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$, is finitely generated; for a [field](c:field) $k$ this holds in $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$.

proofs.name: Ideal of leading coefficients
proofs.slogan: Generate the leading coefficients of an ideal by finitely many polynomials, reduce every element to bounded degree, and finish in a finitely generated module.
proofs.scope: The one-variable step for an arbitrary [ideal](c:ideal) $I$ of $R[x]$, then induction on the number of variables. The zero ideal is generated by the empty set, and $n = 0$ is the hypothesis.

roles.why: Noetherianity makes the leading-coefficient ideal and the bounded-degree module finitely generated.

steps.slogan: Collect the leading coefficients of the polynomials in $I$ into an ideal $L$ of $R$.
steps.detail: Let $L$ hold $0$ and the leading coefficients of the nonzero elements of $I$. If $f, g \in I$ have leading coefficients $a, b$ and degrees $m \le n$, then $x^{n-m} f + g$ and $r f$ lie in $I$ with coefficients $a + b$ in degree $n$ and $ra$ in degree $m$. So $L$ is closed under sums and multiples, and $L$ is an [ideal](c:ideal).

steps.slogan: Choose finitely many polynomials $f_1, \dots, f_k \in I$ whose leading coefficients generate $L$.
steps.detail: Because $R$ is [Noetherian](c:noetherian-ring), $L = (a_1, \dots, a_k)$ for finitely many elements. Choose $f_i \in I$ with leading coefficient $a_i$ and degree $r_i$, and let $r = \max_i r_i$ and $J = (f_1, \dots, f_k) \subseteq I$.

steps.slogan: Lower the degree of each element of $I$ of degree at least $r$ by subtracting multiples of the $f_i$.
steps.detail: If $f \in I$ has degree $m \ge r$ and leading coefficient $a = \sum_i u_i a_i$, then $f - \sum_i u_i x^{m - r_i} f_i$ lies in $I$ and has degree less than $m$. Repetition gives $I = J + (I \cap M)$, where $M$ is the set of polynomials of degree less than $r$.

steps.slogan: Show that $I \cap M$ is a finitely generated $R$-module.
steps.detail: The $R$-module $M$ is generated by $1, x, \dots, x^{r-1}$. A finitely generated module over a Noetherian ring is a [Noetherian module](c:noetherian-module), so its submodule $I \cap M$ is finitely generated.

steps.slogan: Join the generators of $J$ and of $I \cap M$ into a finite generating set of $I$.
steps.detail: The polynomials $f_1, \dots, f_k$ together with module generators of $I \cap M$ generate $J + (I \cap M) = I$ as an ideal. So every ideal of $R[x]$ is finitely generated, and $R[x]$ is Noetherian.

steps.slogan: Add the variables one at a time to reach $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ and $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$.
steps.detail: Since $R[x_1, \dots, x_n] = R[x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}][x_n]$, induction on $n$ with step 5 shows that it is Noetherian. A [field](c:field) has only the ideals $0$ and $k$, so it is Noetherian, and the statement for $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ follows.

concepts.c:noetherian-ring: Noetherianity of $R$ makes the leading-coefficient ideal finitely generated.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The proof adds one polynomial variable at a time.
concepts.c:ideal: The leading coefficients of an ideal of $R[x]$ form an ideal of $R$.
concepts.c:field: A field is Noetherian, so the case over fields follows.
concepts.c:noetherian-module: The bounded-degree part sits in a Noetherian module of polynomials.

source.note: The leading-coefficient proof, as in Atiyah and Macdonald, Introduction to Commutative Algebra, theorem 7.5.

statement: Let $\mu$ be a [probability measure](c:probability-measure), $s$ a closed [convex set](c:convex-set) in a real Banach space $E$, and $g\colon s \to \mathbb{R}$ a continuous [convex function](c:convex-function). If $f$ takes values in $s$ almost everywhere and $f$ and $g \circ f$ are integrable, then $g\left(\int f\, d\mu\right) \le \int g \circ f\, d\mu$: $g$ of the [expected value](c:expected-value) is at most the expected value of $g(f)$.

hypotheses.text: The measure $\mu$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure).
The set $s \subseteq E$ is [convex](c:convex-set) and [closed](c:closed-set), in a real Banach space $E$.
The function $g\colon s \to \mathbb{R}$ is [convex](c:convex-function).
The function $g$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $s$.
The function $f$ takes values in $s$ at $\mu$-almost every point.
The functions $f$ and $g \circ f$ are [integrable](c:integrable-function) for $\mu$.

conclusion: The value of $g$ at the mean is at most the mean of $g$: $g\left(\int f\, d\mu\right) \le \int g(f)\, d\mu$.

proofs.name: Mean in a closed convex epigraph
proofs.slogan: The pair $(f, g \circ f)$ lies in the closed convex epigraph of $g$, and the mean of such a function stays in that set.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The finite version with weights $t_i$ is the case of a measure with finitely many atoms.

roles.why: Total mass $1$ makes the integral of a simple function a convex combination of its values.
Convexity and closedness of $s$ make the epigraph convex and closed.
Convexity of $g$ makes its epigraph convex.
Continuity of $g$ on the closed set $s$ makes the epigraph closed.
Values in $s$ put the pair $(f, g \circ f)$ in the epigraph almost everywhere.
Integrability of $f$ and $g \circ f$ makes the pair integrable, so its mean exists.

steps.slogan: Show that the epigraph $\{(y, t) : y \in s,\ g(y) \le t\}$ is [closed](c:closed-set) and convex.
steps.detail: If $g(y_1) \le t_1$ and $g(y_2) \le t_2$, [convexity](c:convex-function) gives $g(\lambda y_1 + (1 - \lambda) y_2) \le \lambda t_1 + (1 - \lambda) t_2$, so the epigraph is convex. It is closed because $s$ is closed and $g$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $s$.

steps.slogan: Place the integrable pair map $x \mapsto (f(x), g(f(x)))$ in the epigraph almost everywhere.
steps.detail: The pair map is integrable into $E \times \mathbb{R}$ because both components are integrable. For almost every $x$ the point $f(x)$ lies in $s$, so $(f(x), g(f(x)))$ lies in the epigraph.

steps.slogan: Show that a simple function with values in a convex set has its mean in that set.
steps.detail: A simple function takes values $v_1, \dots, v_m$ on sets of measures $t_1, \dots, t_m$ with $\sum t_i = 1$, because $\mu$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure). Its integral $\sum t_i v_i$ is a convex combination, which lies in the convex set.

steps.slogan: Approximate the pair map by simple functions with values in the epigraph and pass to the limit.
steps.detail: Simple functions with values in the epigraph converge to the pair map in $L^1$, so their integrals converge to $\left(\int f, \int g \circ f\right)$. Each of these integrals lies in the epigraph by step 3, and the epigraph is closed, so the limit lies in it.

steps.slogan: Read the second coordinate of the epigraph membership as Jensen's inequality.
steps.detail: The point $\left(\int f\, d\mu, \int g \circ f\, d\mu\right)$ lies in the epigraph, so $\int f\, d\mu \in s$ and $g\left(\int f\, d\mu\right) \le \int g \circ f\, d\mu$.

concepts.c:probability-measure: Total mass one turns integrals of simple functions into convex combinations.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity of $s$ makes the epigraph a convex set.
concepts.c:convex-function: A convex function has a convex epigraph.
concepts.c:closed-set: A closed epigraph keeps the limit of the simple means.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of $g$ makes the epigraph closed.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability makes the mean of the pair map exist.
concepts.c:expected-value: The inequality compares $g$ at the mean with the mean of $g$.

proofs.name: Supporting line at the mean
proofs.slogan: Put a line under the graph of $g$ that touches it at the mean, and integrate the inequality.
proofs.scope: The case $E = \mathbb{R}$, where $s$ is a closed interval. If the mean is an endpoint of $s$, then $f$ equals it almost everywhere and equality holds.

roles.why: Total mass $1$ puts the mean in $s$ and makes the integral of the line equal to its value at the mean.
The convex set $s$ is an interval, which holds the mean of $f$.
Convexity of $g$ gives a supporting line at each interior point of $s$.
A convex function has a supporting line at each interior point without continuity, and the endpoint case needs only $f = m$ almost everywhere.
Values in $s$ put $f$ where the supporting line lies below $g$.
Integrability of $f$ and $g \circ f$ lets the pointwise inequality be integrated.

steps.slogan: Locate the mean $m = \int f\, d\mu$ in the interval $s$.
steps.detail: Since $f \in s$ almost everywhere and $\mu$ has mass $1$, the mean $m$ lies between the endpoints of $s$. If $m$ is an endpoint, say $m = \min s$, then $f - m \ge 0$ has integral $0$, so $f = m$ almost everywhere.

steps.slogan: Settle the endpoint case by the identity $g \circ f = g(m)$ almost everywhere.
steps.detail: If $f = m$ almost everywhere, then $g \circ f = g(m)$ almost everywhere, so $\int g \circ f\, d\mu = g(m)$ and equality holds.

steps.slogan: Draw a supporting line $\ell(y) = g(m) + k(y - m)$ below $g$ at an interior mean.
steps.detail: For a [convex function](c:convex-function), the slopes $(g(y) - g(m))/(y - m)$ increase in $y$. Any $k$ between the left and right limits of these slopes at $m$ gives $g(y) \ge g(m) + k(y - m)$ for every $y \in s$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the inequality $g(f) \ge g(m) + k(f - m)$ over the probability space.
steps.detail: The inequality holds almost everywhere because $f \in s$ almost everywhere. Integration gives $\int g \circ f\, d\mu \ge g(m) + k\left(\int f\, d\mu - m\right) = g(m)$; with step 2 this covers every case.

concepts.c:probability-measure: Mass one makes the integral of the line its value at $m$.
concepts.c:convex-set: A convex subset of the line is an interval that holds the mean.
concepts.c:convex-function: Increasing slopes of a convex function give the supporting line.
concepts.c:closed-set: Closedness is not needed here; the interval holds the mean anyway.
concepts.c:continuous-function: This route needs no continuity, only convexity at the mean.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability lets the pointwise inequality pass through the integral.
concepts.c:expected-value: The supporting line touches the graph exactly at the expected value.

source.note: The classical supporting-line proof for real random variables, as in Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, section 1.6.

statement: Let $H$ be a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space), $V$ a [normed space](c:normed-space) and $B\colon H \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) continuous in its first argument. If $\sup_{\|h\| \le 1} |B(h, v)| \ge c\|v\|$ for all $v \in V$, with $c > 0$, then every continuous [linear functional](c:linear-functional) $f$ on $V$ has some $h \in H$ with $B(h, v) = f(v)$ for all $v$ and $\|h\| \le \|f\|/c$.

hypotheses.text: The space $H$ is a real [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space).
The space $V$ is a real [normed space](c:normed-space).
The map $B\colon H \times V \to \mathbb{R}$ is [bilinear](c:bilinear-form), and $h \mapsto B(h, v)$ is continuous for each $v \in V$.
The form is [coercive](c:coercive-bilinear-form) in the inf-sup sense: $\sup_{\|h\| \le 1} |B(h, v)| \ge c\|v\|$ for every $v \in V$, with $c > 0$.

conclusion: For every continuous [linear functional](c:linear-functional) $f$ on $V$ there is a [weak solution](c:weak-solution) $h \in H$ with $B(h, v) = f(v)$ for all $v \in V$ and $\|h\| \le \|f\|/c$.

proofs.name: Riesz representation and extension
proofs.slogan: Represent the form by an operator $T\colon V \to H$, define the functional $Tv \mapsto f(v)$ on its range, extend it, and represent the extension by a vector.
proofs.scope: The existence direction of Lions's theorem, which gives [weak solutions](c:weak-solution); the solution need not be unique. The converse, from solvability back to the inf-sup bound, is not covered.

roles.why: Completeness and the inner product give the Riesz representation and the orthogonal projection.
The norm of $V$ measures the coercivity bound and the size of $f$.
Continuity in $h$ makes $B(\cdot, v)$ a functional on $H$, and linearity in $v$ makes $T$ linear.
The inf-sup bound gives $\|Tv\| \ge c\|v\|$.

steps.slogan: Represent each functional $B(\cdot, v)$ by a vector $Tv$ of $H$.
steps.detail: For fixed $v$, the map $h \mapsto B(h, v)$ is a continuous [linear functional](c:linear-functional) on $H$, so the Riesz representation theorem gives a unique $Tv \in H$ with $B(h, v) = \langle h, Tv \rangle$ for all $h$. Uniqueness and linearity of $B$ in $v$ make $T\colon V \to H$ linear.

steps.slogan: Turn the coercivity condition into the lower bound $\|Tv\| \ge c\|v\|$.
steps.detail: By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, $\|Tv\| = \sup_{\|h\| \le 1} |\langle h, Tv \rangle| = \sup_{\|h\| \le 1} |B(h, v)|$, which is at least $c\|v\|$ by [coercivity](c:coercive-bilinear-form). In particular $T$ is injective.

steps.slogan: Define the functional $\lambda(Tv) = f(v)$ on the range of $T$.
steps.detail: Injectivity of $T$ makes $\lambda$ well defined and linear on the subspace $W = T(V)$. Step 2 gives $|\lambda(Tv)| \le \|f\|\,\|v\| \le (\|f\|/c)\,\|Tv\|$, so $\lambda$ is bounded on $W$.

steps.slogan: Extend $\lambda$ to all of $H$ without increasing its norm.
steps.detail: Extend $\lambda$ by continuity to the closure $\overline{W}$, and set $\Lambda = \lambda \circ P$ with $P$ the orthogonal projection onto $\overline{W}$. Then $\Lambda$ is a continuous functional on $H$ with $\|\Lambda\| \le \|f\|/c$.

steps.slogan: Represent the extension by a vector $h$ and read off the equation $B(h, v) = f(v)$.
steps.detail: The Riesz representation theorem gives $h \in H$ with $\Lambda(w) = \langle h, w \rangle$ and $\|h\| = \|\Lambda\| \le \|f\|/c$. Then $B(h, v) = \langle h, Tv \rangle = \Lambda(Tv) = f(v)$ for every $v \in V$.

concepts.c:hilbert-space: The Hilbert structure supplies Riesz representation and orthogonal projection.
concepts.c:normed-space: The norm on $V$ measures coercivity and the dual norm of $f$.
concepts.c:bilinear-form: Each slice $B(\cdot, v)$ is a functional that Riesz represents.
concepts.c:coercive-bilinear-form: Coercivity gives the lower bound that makes $T$ injective.
concepts.c:linear-functional: The data $f$ and the slices $B(\cdot, v)$ are linear functionals.
concepts.c:weak-solution: The vector $h$ solves the problem weakly, tested against every $v$.

source.note: The standard Riesz-representation proof of Lions's theorem; for V = H with |B(v, v)| >= c||v||^2 it is the Lax-Milgram proof.

statement: For every integer $r \ge 1$ and all integers $n_1, \dots, n_r \ge 1$ there is an integer $N$ such that every [edge coloring](c:edge-coloring) of the [complete graph](c:complete-graph) $K_N$ with $r$ colors contains, for some $i$, a [clique](c:clique) on $n_i$ vertices whose edges all have color $i$.

hypotheses.text: The number of colors $r$ and the clique sizes $n_1, \dots, n_r$ are positive integers.

conclusion: Some $N = R(n_1, \dots, n_r)$ forces, in every $r$-coloring of the edges of $K_N$, a [clique](c:clique) of size $n_i$ in color $i$ for some $i$.

proofs.name: Neighborhood recursion
proofs.slogan: Split the neighbors of one vertex by color to get $R(s, t) \le R(s - 1, t) + R(s, t - 1)$, then merge colors to handle more than two.
proofs.scope: Two colors by induction on $s + t$, then $r$ colors by induction on $r$. The case $r = 1$ holds with $N = n_1$, and a single vertex is a clique of size $1$ in every color.

roles.why: Positive sizes give the base values $R(s, 1) = R(1, t) = 1$ and a well-founded induction.

steps.slogan: Start the induction with the base values $R(s, 1) = R(1, t) = 1$.
steps.detail: A single vertex has no edges, so it is a [clique](c:clique) of size $1$ in every color. Hence $N = 1$ works whenever one of the two sizes is $1$.

steps.slogan: Split the other vertices by the color of their edge to a fixed vertex $v$.
steps.detail: Let $s, t \ge 2$ and $N = R(s - 1, t) + R(s, t - 1)$, and color the edges of the [complete graph](c:complete-graph) $K_N$ red and blue. The $N - 1$ other vertices split into red and blue neighbors of $v$, and by the pigeonhole principle there are at least $R(s - 1, t)$ red or at least $R(s, t - 1)$ blue neighbors.

steps.slogan: Find the required clique inside the larger color class and add $v$ when needed.
steps.detail: If $v$ has $R(s - 1, t)$ red neighbors, they span a blue $K_t$ or a red $K_{s-1}$, and the red $K_{s-1}$ with $v$ is a red $K_s$; the blue case is symmetric. So $R(s, t) \le R(s - 1, t) + R(s, t - 1)$ is finite by induction on $s + t$.

steps.slogan: Merge the last two colors into one to reduce $r$ colors to $r - 1$ colors.
steps.detail: For $r \ge 3$, treat colors $r - 1$ and $r$ as one color and take $N = R(n_1, \dots, n_{r-2}, R(n_{r-1}, n_r))$, finite by induction on $r$. Either some color $i \le r - 2$ has a $K_{n_i}$, or a merged clique of size $R(n_{r-1}, n_r)$ contains the required clique in color $r - 1$ or $r$.

concepts.c:edge-coloring: The proof splits vertices by the colors of their edges.
concepts.c:complete-graph: Every pair of vertices is joined, so every vertex has $N - 1$ neighbors.
concepts.c:clique: Monochromatic cliques grow by one when the fixed vertex is added.

source.note: The Erdős-Szekeres recursion, as in Diestel, Graph Theory, chapter 9.

statement: Let $X_1, X_2, \dots$ be [independent](c:independent-random-variables), [identically distributed](c:ident-distrib) [random variables](c:random-variable) with values in a finite alphabet and [entropy](c:entropy) $H$ bits. For every $\varepsilon > 0$ and all large $n$, some set of at most $2^{n(H + \varepsilon)}$ words of length $n$ has probability above $1 - \varepsilon$, and every set of at most $2^{n(H - \varepsilon)}$ words has probability below $\varepsilon$.

hypotheses.text: The source symbols $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) and [identically distributed](c:ident-distrib).
The symbols take values in a finite alphabet.

conclusion: Block codes of rate above $H$ bits per symbol have error probability below $\varepsilon$ for large $n$, and codes of rate below $H$ fail with probability above $1 - \varepsilon$.

proofs.name: Typical set
proofs.slogan: The law of large numbers puts almost all probability on about $2^{nH}$ typical words, each of probability about $2^{-nH}$.
proofs.scope: Both parts, for every $\varepsilon > 0$; symbols of probability $0$ are removed first. If $H - \varepsilon < 0$, a set of at most $2^{n(H - \varepsilon)}$ words is empty and the second part is trivial.

roles.why: Independence makes $p(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ a product, and identical laws give one common mean $H$.
A finite alphabet makes $-\log_2 p(X_i)$ bounded, so its mean $H$ is finite.

steps.slogan: Average the information values $-\log_2 p(X_i)$ by the weak law of large numbers.
steps.detail: The variables $Y_i = -\log_2 p(X_i)$ are independent, identically distributed and bounded, with mean $H$. Since $p(X_1, \dots, X_n) = \prod_i p(X_i)$, the law of large numbers gives $-\frac{1}{n}\log_2 p(X_1, \dots, X_n) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i Y_i \to H$ in [probability](c:convergence-in-probability).

steps.slogan: Define the [typical set](c:typical-set) of words with probability between $2^{-n(H+\varepsilon)}$ and $2^{-n(H-\varepsilon)}$.
steps.detail: Let $A_\varepsilon^n$ be the set of words $w$ of length $n$ with $2^{-n(H+\varepsilon)} \le p(w) \le 2^{-n(H-\varepsilon)}$. By step 1, $P((X_1, \dots, X_n) \in A_\varepsilon^n) > 1 - \varepsilon$ for all large $n$.

steps.slogan: Count the typical words by comparing their total probability with $1$.
steps.detail: Each typical word has probability at least $2^{-n(H+\varepsilon)}$, so $1 \ge \sum_{w \in A_\varepsilon^n} p(w) \ge |A_\varepsilon^n|\, 2^{-n(H+\varepsilon)}$. Thus $|A_\varepsilon^n| \le 2^{n(H+\varepsilon)}$, and with step 2 the typical set proves the first part.

steps.slogan: Bound the probability of a small set by its typical part and the atypical rest.
steps.detail: Let $|B| \le 2^{n(H-\varepsilon)}$ and $\delta = \varepsilon/2$. Each word of $A_\delta^n$ has probability at most $2^{-n(H-\delta)}$, so $P(B) \le |B|\, 2^{-n(H-\delta)} + P(\text{not in } A_\delta^n) \le 2^{-n\varepsilon/2} + \varepsilon/2 < \varepsilon$ for large $n$, which is the second part.

steps.slogan: Translate the two set bounds into achievable and impossible code rates.
steps.detail: Index the typical words by binary strings of length $\lceil n(H + \varepsilon) \rceil$ and declare an error outside the typical set; steps 2 and 3 make the error probability less than $\varepsilon$. A code with at most $2^{n(H-\varepsilon)}$ codewords decodes correctly only on a set of that size, which has probability below $\varepsilon$ by step 4.

concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independence turns the word probability into a product of symbol probabilities.
concepts.c:ident-distrib: Identical laws give the information values one common mean.
concepts.c:random-variable: The source is a sequence of random variables on a finite alphabet.
concepts.c:entropy: The entropy is the mean information per symbol and the critical rate.
concepts.c:convergence-in-probability: The empirical information rate converges in probability to the entropy.
concepts.c:typical-set: The typical set carries almost all probability with about $2^{nH}$ words.

source.note: The asymptotic equipartition proof, as in Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, chapter 3.

statement: Let $X$ be a nonempty [compact convex set](c:compact-convex-set) and $Y$ a nonempty convex set, each in a [topological vector space](c:topological-vector-space), and let $f\colon X \times Y \to \mathbb{R}$. If each $f(\cdot, y)$ is lower [semicontinuous](c:semicontinuous-map) and [quasi-convex](c:quasi-convex-function) and each $f(x, \cdot)$ is upper semicontinuous and quasi-concave, then $\min_{x \in X} \sup_{y \in Y} f(x, y) = \sup_{y \in Y} \min_{x \in X} f(x, y)$.

hypotheses.text: The set $X$ is a nonempty [compact convex set](c:compact-convex-set) in a [topological vector space](c:topological-vector-space).
The set $Y$ is a nonempty convex set in a topological vector space.
For each $y \in Y$, the function $f(\cdot, y)$ is lower [semicontinuous](c:semicontinuous-map) and [quasi-convex](c:quasi-convex-function) on $X$.
For each $x \in X$, the function $f(x, \cdot)$ is upper semicontinuous and quasi-concave on $Y$.

conclusion: The minima exist and $\min_{x \in X} \sup_{y \in Y} f(x, y) = \sup_{y \in Y} \min_{x \in X} f(x, y)$.

proofs.name: Komiya's elementary proof
proofs.slogan: Prove the easy inequality between the two sides, then rule out a gap by a two-point lemma, its finite extension and compactness.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, without fixed-point theorems. The inequality $\sup \min \le \min \sup$ holds for every function; the hypotheses give the reverse inequality.

roles.why: Compactness gives the minima and a finite subfamily; convexity makes sublevel sets convex, hence connected.
Convexity of $Y$ puts the segment between two points of $Y$ inside $Y$.
Lower semicontinuity makes sublevel sets in $X$ closed, and quasi-convexity makes them convex.
Quasi-concavity bounds $f(x, \cdot)$ below on a segment, and upper semicontinuity makes the two parts of the segment closed.

steps.slogan: Show that the minima exist and that $\sup_y \min_x f \le \min_x \sup_y f$.
steps.detail: The functions $f(\cdot, y)$ and $\sup_y f(\cdot, y)$ are lower [semicontinuous](c:semicontinuous-map) on the compact set $X$, so they attain their minima. For all $x'$ and $y$, $\min_x f(x, y) \le f(x', y) \le \sup_{y'} f(x', y')$, which gives the inequality.

steps.slogan: Replace two points $y_1, y_2$ that jointly exceed a level $\alpha$ by one point $y_0$.
steps.detail: Suppose $\alpha < \min_x \max(f(x, y_1), f(x, y_2))$ but no $z \in [y_1, y_2]$ has $\min_x f(x, z) > \alpha$, and pick $\beta$ strictly between. Each set $\{x : f(x, z) \le \alpha\}$ is nonempty, convex and so [connected](c:connected-space), and lies in one of the disjoint closed sets $\{f(\cdot, y_i) \le \beta\}$. The two kinds of $z$ split the segment into disjoint nonempty closed sets, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Extend the two-point lemma to finitely many points by induction on their number.
steps.detail: Let $\alpha < \min_x \max_{i \le n} f(x, y_i)$ and $X' = \{x : f(x, y_n) \le \alpha\}$, a compact convex set; if $X'$ is empty, take $y_0 = y_n$. Otherwise induction on $X'$ gives $y'$ with $f(\cdot, y') > \alpha$ on $X'$, so $\max(f(x, y'), f(x, y_n)) > \alpha$ on $X$, and step 2 gives $y_0$.

steps.slogan: Assume a gap $\sup_y \min_x f < \alpha < \min_x \sup_y f$ and select finitely many points $y_i$.
steps.detail: For each $x$ some $y$ has $f(x, y) > \alpha$, so the closed sets $\{x : f(x, y) \le \alpha\}$, $y \in Y$, have empty intersection. Compactness of $X$ gives $y_1, \dots, y_n$ whose sets have empty intersection, that is, $\alpha < \min_x \max_i f(x, y_i)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the finite lemma with the gap to reach a contradiction.
steps.detail: Step 3 gives $y_0$ with $\alpha < \min_x f(x, y_0) \le \sup_y \min_x f$, which contradicts $\sup_y \min_x f < \alpha$. So no gap exists, and with step 1 the two sides are equal.

concepts.c:compact-convex-set: Compactness gives minima and a finite subfamily; convexity gives connected sublevel sets.
concepts.c:topological-vector-space: Segments and convex sets need the linear structure of the space.
concepts.c:semicontinuous-map: Semicontinuity makes the sublevel sets and the segment parts closed.
concepts.c:quasi-convex-function: Quasi-convexity makes each sublevel set convex.
concepts.c:connected-space: A connected segment cannot split into two disjoint closed parts.

source.note: Komiya's proof without fixed points: H. Komiya, Elementary proof for Sion's minimax theorem, Kodai Mathematical Journal 11 (1988), 5-7.

statement: Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a [convex set](c:convex-set) and $x_0$ a [boundary point](c:boundary-point) of $S$. Then a [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) through $x_0$ supports $S$: there is $a \ne 0$ with $a \cdot x \le a \cdot x_0$ for every $x \in S$.

hypotheses.text: The set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is [convex](c:convex-set).
The point $x_0$ is a [boundary point](c:boundary-point) of $S$.

conclusion: Some $a \ne 0$ gives the [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) $\{x : a \cdot x = a \cdot x_0\}$, which contains $x_0$ and has $S$ in the half-space $a \cdot x \le a \cdot x_0$.

proofs.name: Separation from the interior
proofs.slogan: Separate the boundary point from the open convex interior, or place a set with empty interior inside a hyperplane.
proofs.scope: Two cases: $S$ has nonempty [interior](c:interior), or $S$ lies in a proper [affine subspace](c:affine-subspace). The point $x_0$ need not lie in $S$.

roles.why: Convexity makes the interior convex, puts every point of $S$ in the closure of the interior, and puts a set with empty interior in a proper affine subspace.
A boundary point lies outside the interior and in the closure of $S$.

steps.slogan: Place a set with empty interior inside a hyperplane through $x_0$.
steps.detail: If $S$ held $n + 1$ affinely independent points, it would hold their simplex, which has nonempty [interior](c:interior). So $S$ lies in a proper [affine subspace](c:affine-subspace), hence in a closed hyperplane $\{x : a \cdot x = \beta\}$ with $a \ne 0$, and $x_0 \in \overline{S}$ gives $a \cdot x_0 = \beta$.

steps.slogan: Note that $x_0$ lies outside the open convex interior when the interior is nonempty.
steps.detail: If $y$ is an interior point and $x \in S$, then $(1 - t)x + ty$ is an interior point for $0 < t \le 1$, so the interior is convex. A boundary point is not an interior point, so $x_0 \notin \operatorname{int} S$.

steps.slogan: Separate $x_0$ from the interior by a nonzero linear functional.
steps.detail: The Hahn-Banach separation theorem, for the open convex set $\operatorname{int} S$ and the disjoint convex set $\{x_0\}$, gives $a \ne 0$ with $a \cdot x < a \cdot x_0$ for every $x \in \operatorname{int} S$.

steps.slogan: Extend the inequality from the interior to every point of $S$.
steps.detail: For $x \in S$ and an interior point $y$, the points $(1 - t)x + ty$ are interior for $0 < t \le 1$, so $a \cdot ((1 - t)x + ty) < a \cdot x_0$. Letting $t \to 0$ gives $a \cdot x \le a \cdot x_0$.

steps.slogan: Take the hyperplane $a \cdot x = a \cdot x_0$ as the supporting hyperplane in both cases.
steps.detail: In both cases $a \ne 0$, every $x \in S$ has $a \cdot x \le a \cdot x_0$, and $x_0$ lies on the [hyperplane](c:hyperplane). So the hyperplane supports $S$ at the [boundary point](c:boundary-point) $x_0$.

concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity of $S$ makes its interior convex and dense in $S$.
concepts.c:boundary-point: The boundary point is where the hyperplane touches the set.
concepts.c:hyperplane: The supporting hyperplane is a level set of the separating functional.
concepts.c:interior: The proof separates $x_0$ from the open interior of $S$.
concepts.c:affine-subspace: A convex set with empty interior lies in a proper affine subspace.

source.note: The separation proof, as in Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, section 2.5.2.

statement:
Let $(X, \mu)$ and $(Y, 
u)$ be [σ-finite](c:sigma-finite-measure) measure spaces and $f\colon X 	imes Y 	o [0, \infty]$ a [measurable](c:measurable-function) function. Then $x \mapsto \int_Y f(x, y)\, d
u(y)$ is measurable, and $\int_{X 	imes Y} f\, d(\mu 	imes 
u) = \int_X \int_Y f\, d
u\, d\mu = \int_Y \int_X f\, d\mu\, d
u$ for the [product measure](c:product-measure) $\mu 	imes 
u$.

hypotheses.text: The measures $\mu$ and $\nu$ are [σ-finite](c:sigma-finite-measure).
The function $f$ is [measurable](c:measurable-function) for the product σ-algebra.
The function $f$ is [nonnegative](c:nonnegative-measurable-function), with values in $[0, \infty]$.

conclusion: The inner integrals are measurable, and the integral over $X \times Y$ equals both iterated integrals, finite or infinite.

formal.difference: The declaration gives only the order $\int_X \int_Y$, assumes only that $\nu$ is s-finite and $f$ almost everywhere measurable, and omits the measurability of the inner integral. The other order is MeasureTheory.lintegral_prod_symm.

proofs.name: Slice measures and monotone approximation
proofs.slogan: Write the product measure through the measures of slices, extend the formula from indicators to simple functions, and pass to the limit by monotone convergence.
proofs.scope: Both iterated orders; no integrability is needed, because both sides may be $+\infty$. The second order comes from the first by swapping the factors.

roles.why: σ-finiteness of $\nu$ makes slice measures measurable in $x$, and σ-finiteness of both measures makes the product symmetric.
Measurability gives measurable slices and increasing simple measurable approximations.
Nonnegativity makes the approximations increase, so monotone convergence applies without integrability.

steps.slogan: Show that $x \mapsto \nu(E_x)$ is measurable for every measurable set $E \subseteq X \times Y$.
steps.detail: For finite $\nu$, the sets $E$ with this property contain the measurable rectangles and form a Dynkin system, so they form the whole product σ-algebra by the π-λ theorem. A [σ-finite](c:sigma-finite-measure) $\nu$ is a countable sum of finite measures, which keeps measurability.

steps.slogan: Express the [product measure](c:product-measure) as $(\mu \times \nu)(E) = \int_X \nu(E_x)\, d\mu(x)$.
steps.detail: The right side is a measure in $E$ by monotone convergence, and on rectangles it equals $\mu(A)\nu(B)$. It is therefore the product measure; mathlib takes this formula, as a bind of the slice measures, as the definition.

steps.slogan: Extend the formula from indicator functions to nonnegative [simple functions](c:simple-function) by linearity.
steps.detail: For $f = 1_E$, step 2 is the claim, because $\int_Y 1_E(x, y)\, d\nu(y) = \nu(E_x)$. Both sides are additive and positively homogeneous in $f$, so the formula holds for finite sums $\sum c_k 1_{E_k}$ with $c_k \ge 0$.

steps.slogan: Approximate $f$ from below by simple functions and pass to the limit three times.
steps.detail: Take simple $f_k \uparrow f$. Monotone convergence gives $\int_Y f_k(x, \cdot)\, d\nu \uparrow \int_Y f(x, \cdot)\, d\nu$ for each $x$, so the inner integral is measurable, and then convergence of the outer integrals and of the product integrals carries the formula to $f$.

steps.slogan: Swap the two factors to get the second iterated order.
steps.detail:
For σ-finite $\mu$ and $
u$, the swap map $(x, y) \mapsto (y, x)$ carries $\mu 	imes 
u$ to $
u 	imes \mu$, because both measures agree on rectangles. Steps 1 to 4 for $f$ composed with the swap give $\int_{X 	imes Y} f = \int_Y \int_X f\, d\mu\, d
u$.

concepts.c:sigma-finite-measure: σ-finiteness gives measurable slice measures and a symmetric product.
concepts.c:measurable-function: Measurable functions are increasing limits of simple measurable functions.
concepts.c:nonnegative-measurable-function: Nonnegativity lets monotone convergence replace any integrability condition.
concepts.c:product-measure: The product measure is the integral of the slice measures.
concepts.c:simple-function: Simple functions carry the formula from sets to general functions.

source.note: mathlib defines μ.prod ν as a bind of the slice measures (measurable by measurable_measure_prodMk_left) and rewrites with lintegral_bind and lintegral_map; lintegral_bind rests on lintegral_join, which uses simple-function approximation (lintegral_eq_iSup_eapprox_lintegral).

statement: Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be an open [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space) set and $f\colon U \to \mathbb{C}$ a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function). Then the [contour integral](c:contour-integral) $\oint_\gamma f(z)\, dz$ is $0$ for every closed piecewise smooth curve $\gamma$ in $U$.

hypotheses.text: The set $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is open and [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space).
The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on $U$.
The curve $\gamma$ is closed and piecewise smooth, with image in $U$.

proofs.name: Goursat, local primitives and homotopy
proofs.slogan: Kill rectangle integrals by repeated quartering, build primitives on disks, and deform the curve to a point through small squares.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with no continuity assumption on $f'$. The constant curve, whose integral is $0$, ends the deformation.

roles.why: Openness gives disks around each point, and simple connectivity gives a homotopy from $\gamma$ to a constant curve.
Complex differentiability at the limit point of nested rectangles makes rectangle integrals vanish.
The closed curve is the object that the homotopy deforms.

steps.slogan: Show by repeated quartering that $f$ integrates to $0$ over every rectangle boundary in $U$.
steps.detail: If a closed rectangle $R \subset U$ has $|\oint_{\partial R} f| = \eta$, one of its four quarters has integral at least $\eta/4$; nesting gives rectangles $R_k$ shrinking to a point $z_0$ with $|\oint_{\partial R_k} f| \ge 4^{-k}\eta$. The expansion $f(z) = f(z_0) + f'(z_0)(z - z_0) + o(|z - z_0|)$ bounds this by $o(4^{-k})$, so $\eta = 0$.

steps.slogan: Build a [primitive](c:antiderivative) of $f$ on every disk in $U$ along axis-parallel paths.
steps.detail: On a disk $D \subseteq U$ with center $c$, let $F(z)$ be the integral of $f$ along the horizontal then vertical path from $c$ to $z$. Step 1 shows that $F(z + h) - F(z)$ is the integral over a short path from $z$ to $z + h$, so $F' = f$ and every closed curve in $D$ has integral $0$.

steps.slogan: Show that homotopic closed curves give equal integrals by cutting the homotopy into small squares.
steps.detail: Let $H\colon [0, 1]^2 \to U$ be a [homotopy](c:homotopy) of closed curves. Uniform continuity cuts the square into small squares whose images lie in disks of $U$; each small boundary loop has integral $0$ by step 2, and the interior edges cancel in the sum.

steps.slogan: Contract $\gamma$ to a constant curve inside the simply connected set $U$.
steps.detail: Since $U$ is [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space), $\gamma$ is homotopic in $U$ to a constant curve, whose integral is $0$. Step 3 gives $\oint_\gamma f(z)\, dz = 0$.

concepts.c:simply-connected-space: Simple connectivity lets $\gamma$ shrink to a point inside $U$.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Complex differentiability makes the linear approximation integrate to zero.
concepts.c:contour-integral: The proof shows that the contour integral vanishes on closed curves.
concepts.c:antiderivative: A local primitive makes integrals over small loops vanish.
concepts.c:homotopy: Homotopy invariance moves the integral from $\gamma$ to a constant curve.

source.note: Goursat's theorem, local primitives and homotopy invariance, as in Stein and Shakarchi, Complex Analysis, chapters 2 and 3.

proofs.name: Green's theorem and Cauchy-Riemann
proofs.slogan: Turn the contour integral into area integrals by Green's theorem, where the Cauchy-Riemann equations make the integrands vanish.
proofs.scope: Cauchy's original setting: $f'$ is continuous and $\gamma$ is a positively oriented simple closed curve. Simple connectivity puts the region $D$ inside $\gamma$ into $U$.

roles.why: Simple connectivity places the region inside $\gamma$ in $U$, where $f$ is holomorphic.
Holomorphy gives the [Cauchy-Riemann equations](c:cauchy-riemann-equations) for $u$ and $v$.
The closed curve bounds the region of Green's theorem.

steps.slogan: Write $f = u + iv$ and split the contour integral into two real line integrals.
steps.detail: With $dz = dx + i\, dy$, $\oint_\gamma f\, dz = \oint_\gamma (u\, dx - v\, dy) + i \oint_\gamma (v\, dx + u\, dy)$. Both are line integrals of real $C^1$ forms because $f'$ is continuous.

steps.slogan: Turn each line integral into a double integral over the inside region $D$ by Green's theorem.
steps.detail: Green's theorem $\oint (P\, dx + Q\, dy) = \iint_D (Q_x - P_y)\, dA$ applies because $\overline{D} \subset U$. It gives $\oint_\gamma f\, dz = \iint_D (-v_x - u_y)\, dA + i \iint_D (u_x - v_y)\, dA$.

steps.slogan: Cancel both integrands with the Cauchy-Riemann equations $u_x = v_y$ and $u_y = -v_x$.
steps.detail: A [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) satisfies the [Cauchy-Riemann equations](c:cauchy-riemann-equations), so $-v_x - u_y = 0$ and $u_x - v_y = 0$ on $D$. Both double integrals vanish, and $\oint_\gamma f(z)\, dz = 0$.

concepts.c:simply-connected-space: Simple connectivity keeps the inside region of $\gamma$ within $U$.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy supplies the Cauchy-Riemann equations on the region.
concepts.c:contour-integral: The contour integral splits into two real line integrals.
concepts.c:cauchy-riemann-equations: The equations make both Green integrands identically zero.

source.note: Cauchy's original argument through Green's theorem, as in Brown and Churchill, Complex Variables and Applications, the section on the Cauchy-Goursat theorem.

statement: Let $s \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a [measurable set](c:measurable-set) and $f\colon s \to \mathbb{R}^n$ an [injective](c:injective-map) map, [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) on $s$ with [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix) $Df(x)$. Then $\int_{f(s)} g(y)\, dy = \int_s |\det Df(x)|\, g(f(x))\, dx$ for every function $g$ integrable on $f(s)$, with [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) on both sides.

hypotheses.text: The set $s \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is [Lebesgue measurable](c:measurable-set).
The map $f\colon s \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is [differentiable](c:differentiable-function) at each point of $s$, relative to $s$, with derivative $Df(x)$.
The map $f$ is [injective](c:injective-map) on $s$.

conclusion: The integral of $g$ over $f(s)$ equals the integral over $s$ of $g \circ f$ weighted by the absolute [determinant](c:determinant) $|\det Df(x)|$.

formal.difference: The declaration uses any additive Haar measure on a finite-dimensional real normed space and any $g$ with values in a Banach space. It states the equality for every $g$, with the convention that a non-integrable function has integral $0$.

proofs.name: Local linearization of the image measure
proofs.slogan: Compute the measure of images first for linear maps, then for pieces where $f$ is nearly linear, and transfer the measure identity to integrals.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Points where $\det Df(x) = 0$ need no separate case: their image has measure zero, which matches the zero weight.

roles.why: Measurability of $s$ lets it be cut into measurable pieces and makes $f$ a measurable embedding.
Differentiability makes $f$ close to a linear map on small pieces.
Injectivity makes the images of disjoint pieces disjoint, so their measures add.

steps.slogan: Scale the [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) of every set by $|\det A|$ under a linear map $A$.
steps.detail: The measure $t \mapsto \lambda(A(t))$ is translation invariant, so it is a constant multiple of $\lambda$. Row reduction writes $A$ as a product of elementary maps, and a check on the unit cube shows that the constant is $|\det A|$, with $0$ for singular $A$.

steps.slogan: Cut $s$ into countably many pieces on which $f$ stays close to a linear map.
steps.detail: For $\varepsilon > 0$, choose linear maps $A_k$ and measurable pieces $t_k$ covering $s$ with $\|f(x) - f(y) - A_k(x - y)\| \le \varepsilon\|x - y\|$ and $\|Df(x) - A_k\| \le \varepsilon$ on $t_k$. [Differentiability](c:differentiable-function) at each point and separability of the space of linear maps give such a countable cover.

steps.slogan: Compare the measure of each image piece with $|\det A_k|$ times the measure of the piece.
steps.detail: On a piece where $f$ is $\varepsilon$-close to $A_k$, step 1 gives $\lambda(f(t)) \le (|\det A_k| + \eta)\,\lambda(t)$ and, for invertible $A_k$, $\lambda(f(t)) \ge (|\det A_k| - \eta)\,\lambda(t)$, with $\eta \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. The weight $|\det Df|$ differs from $|\det A_k|$ by at most $\eta$ there.

steps.slogan: Sum over the pieces and let $\varepsilon \to 0$ to get $\lambda(f(t)) = \int_t |\det Df|\, d\lambda$.
steps.detail: Injectivity makes the images $f(t \cap t_k)$ disjoint, so their measures add, and the errors sum to at most $\eta$ times the measure. Letting $\varepsilon \to 0$ gives the identity for every measurable $t \subseteq s$: $f$ carries the measure $|\det Df|\,\lambda$ on $s$ to $\lambda$ on $f(s)$.

steps.slogan: Transfer the measure identity to integrals of $g$ through the measurable embedding $f$.
steps.detail: An injective map that is differentiable on a measurable set is a measurable embedding of that set. Integration against an image measure is integration of the composite, so $\int_{f(s)} g\, d\lambda = \int_s g(f(x))\, |\det Df(x)|\, dx$.

concepts.c:measurable-set: Measurable pieces of $s$ carry the local comparison.
concepts.c:injective-map: Injectivity makes the image pieces disjoint, so their measures add.
concepts.c:jacobian-matrix: The Jacobian is the linear map that approximates $f$ on each piece.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: The proof computes how $f$ distorts Lebesgue measure.
concepts.c:determinant: The absolute determinant is the volume factor of a linear map.
concepts.c:differentiable-function: Differentiability gives pieces where $f$ is nearly linear.

statement: For [integrable](c:integrable-function) $f, g\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$, the [convolution](c:convolution) $(f * g)(x) = \int f(x - y)\, g(y)\, dy$ is integrable, and its [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) is the product of the transforms: $\widehat{f * g}(\xi) = \hat f(\xi)\, \hat g(\xi)$ for every $\xi$, where $\hat f(\xi) = \int f(x)\, e^{-2\pi i x \cdot \xi}\, dx$.

hypotheses.text: The functions $f$ and $g$ are [integrable](c:integrable-function) on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

conclusion: The convolution $f * g$ is integrable and $\widehat{f * g} = \hat f\, \hat g$ everywhere.

proofs.name: Fubini and a translation
proofs.slogan: Write the transform of the convolution as a double integral, swap the order by Fubini's theorem, and shift the inner variable.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for every $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^n$. The convolution is defined for almost every $x$, which suffices for its transform.

roles.why: Integrability of $f$ and $g$ makes the double integral absolutely convergent.

steps.slogan: Show by Tonelli's theorem that $\iint |f(x - y)|\,|g(y)|\, dy\, dx = \|f\|_1 \|g\|_1$.
steps.detail: Tonelli's theorem allows integration in $x$ first, and translation invariance of [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) gives $\int |f(x - y)|\, dx = \|f\|_1$. So the [convolution](c:convolution) integral converges absolutely for almost every $x$, and $\|f * g\|_1 \le \|f\|_1 \|g\|_1$.

steps.slogan: Write $\widehat{f * g}(\xi)$ as a double integral and swap its order by Fubini's theorem.
steps.detail: $\widehat{f * g}(\xi) = \int \left(\int f(x - y)\, g(y)\, dy\right) e^{-2\pi i x \cdot \xi}\, dx$. The integrand has absolute value $|f(x - y)|\,|g(y)|$, integrable on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ by step 1, so Fubini's theorem puts the $x$ integral inside.

steps.slogan: Substitute $x = u + y$ in the inner integral to split off the factor $e^{-2\pi i y \cdot \xi}$.
steps.detail: Translation invariance gives $\int f(x - y)\, e^{-2\pi i x \cdot \xi}\, dx = e^{-2\pi i y \cdot \xi} \int f(u)\, e^{-2\pi i u \cdot \xi}\, du = \hat f(\xi)\, e^{-2\pi i y \cdot \xi}$, because the exponential of a sum is the product of the exponentials.

steps.slogan: Integrate the remaining factor against $g$ to obtain $\hat f(\xi)\, \hat g(\xi)$.
steps.detail: The outer integral is $\int g(y)\, \hat f(\xi)\, e^{-2\pi i y \cdot \xi}\, dy = \hat f(\xi)\, \hat g(\xi)$, which converges because $g$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function).

concepts.c:convolution: The convolution is the inner integral that the proof unfolds.
concepts.c:fourier-transform: The exponential in the transform splits into a product after the shift.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability makes the double integral absolutely convergent.
concepts.c:lebesgue-measure: Translation invariance of Lebesgue measure justifies the shift $x = u + y$.

source.note: The standard Fubini argument, as in Folland, Real Analysis, chapter 8.

statement: Let $f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be [continuous](c:continuous-function), with $a < b$. Then the [integral](c:riemann-integral) function $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\, dt$ has [derivative](c:derivative) $F'(x) = f(x)$ on $[a, b]$, one-sided at the ends, and every [antiderivative](c:antiderivative) $G$ of $f$ satisfies $\int_a^b f(t)\, dt = G(b) - G(a)$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $[a, b]$, with $a < b$.
The function $G$ is an [antiderivative](c:antiderivative) of $f$: it is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $G'(x) = f(x)$ for $a < x < b$.

conclusion: The integral function has $F' = f$ on $[a, b]$, and $\int_a^b f(t)\, dt = G(b) - G(a)$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only the first part, at the right end $b$, in a stronger form: $f$ need only be integrable with an almost-everywhere limit $c$ at $b$, and the derivative is strict. The second part is the separate declaration intervalIntegral.integral_eq_sub_of_hasDeriv_right_of_le.

proofs.name: Local averages and the mean value theorem
proofs.slogan: Bound the difference quotient of $F$ by the oscillation of $f$ near $x$, then show that $G - F$ is constant.
proofs.scope: Both parts. At the ends $a$ and $b$ the same estimate gives one-sided derivatives.

roles.why: Continuity makes $f$ integrable and makes $f(t)$ close to $f(x)$ for $t$ near $x$.
The antiderivative has the same derivative as $F$ inside the interval and is continuous at the ends.

steps.slogan: Write the increment of $F$ minus $h f(x)$ as an integral of $f(t) - f(x)$.
steps.detail: Additivity of the [integral](c:riemann-integral) over adjacent intervals gives $F(x + h) - F(x) - h f(x) = \int_x^{x+h} (f(t) - f(x))\, dt$ whenever $x$ and $x + h$ lie in $[a, b]$. The integral exists because a continuous function on $[a, b]$ is integrable.

steps.slogan: Bound this integral by $\varepsilon |h|$ to obtain $F'(x) = f(x)$.
steps.detail: Given $\varepsilon > 0$, [continuity](c:continuous-function) at $x$ gives $\delta > 0$ with $|f(t) - f(x)| < \varepsilon$ for $|t - x| < \delta$. For $0 < |h| < \delta$ the integral in step 1 is at most $\varepsilon |h|$, so the difference quotient of $F$ tends to $f(x)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $G - F$ is constant by the mean value theorem.
steps.detail: The function $H = G - F$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and has [derivative](c:derivative) $f - f = 0$ on $(a, b)$ by step 2. For $a \le x < y \le b$ the mean value theorem gives $H(y) - H(x) = H'(\xi)(y - x) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the constant difference at the ends to get $\int_a^b f = G(b) - G(a)$.
steps.detail: Since $H(b) = H(a)$, the difference is $G(b) - G(a) = F(b) - F(a) = \int_a^b f(t)\, dt - 0$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity at $x$ makes the local average of $f$ tend to $f(x)$.
concepts.c:derivative: The proof computes the derivative of the integral function.
concepts.c:antiderivative: Two antiderivatives of the same function differ by a constant.
concepts.c:riemann-integral: Additivity of the integral over intervals expresses the increment of $F$.

proofs.name: Telescoping Riemann sums
proofs.slogan: Telescope $G(b) - G(a)$ over a partition, replace each difference by the mean value theorem, and recognize a Riemann sum of $f$.
proofs.scope: The second part only; the first part needs the local-average proof. The proof uses only that $f$ is Riemann integrable, which continuity gives.

roles.why: Continuity makes $f$ Riemann integrable, so the Riemann sums converge to the integral.
The antiderivative supplies the mean value points on each subinterval.

steps.slogan: Write $G(b) - G(a)$ as a telescoping sum over a partition of $[a, b]$.
steps.detail: For a partition $a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_m = b$, $G(b) - G(a) = \sum_{k=1}^m (G(x_k) - G(x_{k-1}))$, because the intermediate terms cancel.

steps.slogan: Replace each difference by $f(\xi_k)(x_k - x_{k-1})$ with the mean value theorem.
steps.detail: On $[x_{k-1}, x_k]$ the [antiderivative](c:antiderivative) $G$ is continuous and differentiable inside with [derivative](c:derivative) $G' = f$. The mean value theorem gives $\xi_k \in (x_{k-1}, x_k)$ with $G(x_k) - G(x_{k-1}) = f(\xi_k)(x_k - x_{k-1})$.

steps.slogan: Recognize $G(b) - G(a)$ as a Riemann sum of $f$ for every partition.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 give $G(b) - G(a) = \sum_k f(\xi_k)(x_k - x_{k-1})$, a Riemann sum of $f$ with tags $\xi_k$. This holds for every partition, with suitable tags.

steps.slogan: Refine the partitions so that the Riemann sums tend to the integral.
steps.detail: A [continuous](c:continuous-function) function on $[a, b]$ is uniformly continuous, hence Riemann integrable, so the Riemann sums tend to the [integral](c:riemann-integral) $\int_a^b f(t)\, dt$ as the mesh tends to $0$. They all equal $G(b) - G(a)$, so the limit is $G(b) - G(a)$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity gives uniform continuity and so Riemann integrability.
concepts.c:derivative: The derivative $G' = f$ enters through the mean value points.
concepts.c:antiderivative: The increments of the antiderivative telescope to $G(b) - G(a)$.
concepts.c:riemann-integral: The integral is the limit of Riemann sums that all equal $G(b) - G(a)$.

source.note: The Riemann-sum proof, as in Spivak, Calculus, chapter 14.

statement: Let $(A_i)_{i \in I}$ be a family of [finite sets](c:finite-set). There is an [injective](c:injective-map) choice $i \mapsto a_i \in A_i$ if and only if every finite $J \subseteq I$ satisfies $|J| \le |\bigcup_{i \in J} A_i|$. In the [bipartite graph](c:bipartite-graph) of indices and elements, such a choice is a [matching](c:matching) that covers $I$.

hypotheses.text: Each set $A_i$ is [finite](c:finite-set); the index set $I$ is arbitrary.

conclusion: An injective choice $a_i \in A_i$ exists exactly when Hall's condition $|J| \le |\bigcup_{i \in J} A_i|$ holds for every finite $J \subseteq I$.

proofs.name: Induction and compactness
proofs.slogan: Prove the finite case by induction with a split at a critical subfamily, then pass to infinite families through an inverse limit of finite sets.
proofs.scope: Necessity is direct. Sufficiency is proved first for finite $I$ by strong induction on $|I|$, with $I = \emptyset$ trivial, and then for arbitrary $I$ by compactness.

roles.why: Finite sets make the set of matchings on each finite subfamily finite, which the compactness step needs.

steps.slogan: Show that an injective choice forces Hall's condition.
steps.detail: If $i \mapsto a_i$ is [injective](c:injective-map) with $a_i \in A_i$, then for finite $J$ the set $\{a_i : i \in J\}$ has $|J|$ elements and lies in $\bigcup_{i \in J} A_i$.

steps.slogan: Match one index freely when every proper subfamily has a surplus.
steps.detail: Let $I$ be finite and nonempty, with $|\bigcup_{i \in J} A_i| \ge |J| + 1$ for every nonempty proper $J \subset I$. Choose $i_0$ and $a \in A_{i_0}$; removing $i_0$ and deleting $a$ from the other sets keeps Hall's condition, and induction matches the rest.

steps.slogan: Split at a critical subfamily $J$ with $|\bigcup_{i \in J} A_i| = |J|$.
steps.detail: Induction matches $J$ into $U = \bigcup_{i \in J} A_i$. For $K \subseteq I \setminus J$, the sets $A_i \setminus U$ satisfy $|\bigcup_{i \in K} (A_i \setminus U)| \ge |K \cup J| - |U| = |K|$, so induction matches $I \setminus J$ outside $U$, and the two matchings combine.

steps.slogan: Form the [inverse system](c:inverse-system) of matchings on the finite subfamilies of $I$.
steps.detail: For finite $J \subseteq I$, let $M(J)$ be the set of injective choices on $J$. It is nonempty by steps 2 and 3 and finite because each $A_i$ is [finite](c:finite-set); restriction maps $M(J') \to M(J)$ for $J \subseteq J'$ make an inverse system.

steps.slogan: Take a compatible family of matchings from the nonempty inverse limit.
steps.detail: Give each finite $M(J)$ the discrete topology, so the product $\prod_J M(J)$ is compact by Tychonoff's theorem. The families compatible on finitely many pairs $J \subseteq J'$ form closed sets with the finite intersection property, so some family is compatible everywhere.

steps.slogan: Read off an injective choice from the compatible family and combine both directions.
steps.detail: Let $a_i$ be the value at $i$ of the matching on $\{i\}$. Compatibility on $\{i, i'\}$ gives $a_i \ne a_{i'}$ for $i \ne i'$, and $a_i \in A_i$; with step 1 this proves the equivalence.

concepts.c:finite-set: Finite sets make each set of partial matchings finite and compact.
concepts.c:injective-map: The required choice of representatives is an injective map.
concepts.c:bipartite-graph: The family is a bipartite graph between indices and elements.
concepts.c:matching: An injective choice is a matching that covers every index.
concepts.c:inverse-system: Matchings on finite subfamilies form an inverse system under restriction.
